summary: Defines MULE, an application protocol that transfers Internet mail messages over ACP 142 P_MUL, a reliable multicast protocol for bandwidth-constrained, delayed-acknowledgement environments running over UDP.

eli5.summary: It lets one email be sent to many receivers at once over a slow radio link, like a loudspeaker rather than many phone calls.

questions: how does email work on radio networks
subtitle: Send email to many receivers at once over bandwidth-limited radio networks.

tldr.problem: Email systems need to send messages to many recipients over bandwidth-constrained radio networks where receivers cannot immediately acknowledge receipt.
tldr.mechanism: MULE uses P_MUL, a reliable multicast protocol that sends one email to multiple recipients in a single transmission over UDP, with compressed payload and support for SMTP extensions.
tldr.outcome: Saves bandwidth compared to separate unicast transmissions, enabling email transfer between mail servers in radio and military network environments.

today: RFC 8494 is an Informational specification describing an existing implementation. It is not an Internet Standard, but documents how multicast email transfer works in military and radio network environments.

sections.title: Why MULE Exists
sections.content:
P_MUL is a reliable multicast protocol designed for difficult network conditions: when bandwidth is scarce and receiving nodes cannot immediately acknowledge messages for long periods (a state called EMCON, or radio silence). MULE applies this protocol to Internet email, letting Message Transfer Agents (MTAs) send the same email to multiple recipients with a single transmission instead of repeating it for each destination.

This is useful in military and radio network settings where sending the same message multiple times wastes precious bandwidth. One transmission reaches all receivers, even if they cannot respond right away.
sections.eli5: In normal email, sending one message to three people means three separate transmissions. MULE sends once and all three receive it, saving bandwidth on slow radio links.

sections.title: The Message Envelope
sections.content:
MULE packages email in a BSMTP-like payload, a simplified version of Batch SMTP that removes unnecessary protocol steps. Since EMCON conditions prevent real-time negotiation, the payload includes no capability announcements.

The envelope contains a sender address with optional SMTP extension parameters (like message priority), followed by one line for each recipient with their address and parameters. An empty line marks the end of the recipient list, and the message body follows. No transparency encoding or special termination is needed because the ACP 142 framing shows where the message ends.
sections.eli5: The message envelope is a list: sender, recipients, then the actual email. It skips the back-and-forth talking that normal SMTP does.

sections.title: Compression and Transport
sections.content:
The BSMTP-like payload is compressed using zlib before transmission. The compressed data is wrapped in an ASN.1 CompressedData structure with a content type identifier set to 25 (the MULE value). The structure is then encoded using BER (Basic Encoding Rules) and sent as P_MUL Protocol Data Units (PDUs).

When a message has priority information (from the MT-PRIORITY SMTP extension), that priority is mapped to an ACP 142 priority field using the formula 6 - priority_value to ensure proper ordering in the multicast delivery.
sections.eli5: The message gets squashed down (compressed) to fit through radio links, then wrapped in a special container that says 'this is MULE email' and sent out.

sections.title: Gateways Between MULE and Internet Email
sections.content:
Gateways bridge MULE and traditional SMTP networks. An SMTP-to-MULE gateway receives email over SMTP and relays it through P_MUL by creating the BSMTP-like payload, compressing it, and sending it as P_MUL messages. A MULE-to-SMTP gateway does the reverse: it receives compressed MULE messages, decompresses them, extracts the recipient list, and submits the email via SMTP to the next hop.

When SMTP includes the CHUNKING extension (binary message transfer in chunks), the gateway reassembles the message into its complete form before converting it to MULE format. The BODY=BINARY parameter in the envelope indicates binary content.
sections.eli5: A gateway is a translator. It takes email from one world (SMTP) and rewrites it for the other (MULE), or vice versa, handling compression and formatting.

sections.title: Delivery Status and Errors
sections.content:
MULE requires MTAs to support certain SMTP extensions: SIZE, 8BITMIME, DSN, MT-PRIORITY, DELIVER-BY, BINARYMIME, and CHUNKING. Unlike SMTP, MULE cannot return immediate response codes because multicast and EMCON conditions prevent interactive feedback.

When a receiving MTA cannot deliver a message to the final recipients, it generates a Delivery Status Notification (DSN) report and submits it back to the sender using MULE. Some SMTP extensions (like PIPELINING and STARTTLS) are not applicable to MULE because they require real-time communication. Others (like CHECKPOINT) are incompatible because they would interrupt the MULE transaction flow.
sections.eli5: When something goes wrong, the server can't ask 'Did you get it?' so it sends an error report back via MULE instead of a real-time response.
